4.6. Scheduling, Organization and Team Structures
Project-task scheduling is an important project planning activity. It involves deciding which tasks would
be taken up when. In order to schedule the project activities, a software project manager needs to do
the following:
• Identify all the tasks needed to complete the project and Break down large tasks into small
activities.
• Determine the dependency among different activities and Establish the most likely estimates
for the time durations necessary to complete the activities and Allocate resources to activities.
• Plan the starting and ending dates for various activities and Determine the critical path. A
critical path is the chain of activities that determines the duration of the project.

module_refs.quote:
A class in an object-oriented system carefully delineates between its interfaces the routines and
attributes within a class are held together tightly. In a properly designed system, the classes will
be grouped into subsystems but remain independent; therefore, changing one class has no impact
on other classes, and so, the impact is minimized. However, the object-oriented approach is not a
panacea; nothing is magical here that will promote perfect design or perfect code.
Promotion of reusability
Objects are reusable because they are modeled directly out of a real-world problem domain. Each
object stands by itself or within a small circle of peers (other objects). Within this framework, the
class does not concern itself with the rest of the system or how it is going to be used within a
particular system.

6.1.3. Coupling and coherence
Coupling is the strength of dependencies between two subsystems. If two subsystems are loosely
coupled, they are relatively independent, and thus, modifications to one of the subsystems will
have little impact on the other. If two subsystems are strongly coupled, modifications to one
subsystem is likely to have impact on the other. A desirable property of a subsystem decomposition
is that subsystems are as loosely coupled as possible. This minimizes the impact that errors or
future changes have on the correct operation of the system.

module_refs.title: Software Engineering module
module_refs.quote:
Requirement’s elicitation focuses on describing the purpose of the system. The client, the
developers, and the users identify a problem area and define a system that addresses the problem.
Such a definition is called a system specification and serves as a contract between the client and
the developers. The system specification is structured and formalized during analysis to produce
an analysis model (see Figure 3.1). Both system specification and analysis model represent the
same information. They differ only in the language and notation they use. The system specification
is written in natural language, whereas the analysis model is usually expressed in a formal or
semiformal notation.

module_refs.title: Software Engineering module
module_refs.quote:
Analysis focuses on producing a model of the system, called the analysis model, which is correct,
complete, consistent, and verifiable. Analysis is different from requirements elicitation in that
developers focus on structuring and formalizing the requirements elicited from users
Figure 4.1 Products of requirements elicitation and analysis (UML activity diagram).
Althoughtheanalysismodelmaynotbeunderstandabletotheusersandtheclient, it helps developers
verify the system specification produced during requirements elicitation. There is a natural
tendency for users and developers to postpone difficult decisions until later in the project. A
decision may be difficult because of lack of domain knowledge, lack of technological knowledge,

6.1.2. Services and subsystem interfaces
A subsystem is characterized by the services it provides to other subsystems. A service is a set of
related operations that share a common purpose. A subsystem providing a notification service, for
example, defines operations to send notices, look up notification channels, and subscribe and
unsubscribe to a channel.
The set of operations of a subsystem that are available to other subsystems form the subsystem
interface. The subsystem interface, also referred to as the application programmer interface (API),
includes the name of the operations, their parameters, their types, and their return values. System
design focuses on defining the services provided by each subsystem that is, enumerating the
operations, their parameters, and their high-level behavior. Object design will focus on defining
the subsystem interfaces, that is, the type of the parameters and the return value of each operation.
The definition of a subsystem in terms of the services it provides helps us focus on its interface as
opposed to its implementation. A good subsystem interface should provide as little information

module_refs.title: Software Engineering module
module_refs.quote:
6.1.3. Coupling and coherence
Coupling is the strength of dependencies between two subsystems. If two subsystems are loosely
coupled, they are relatively independent, and thus, modifications to one of the subsystems will
have little impact on the other. If two subsystems are strongly coupled, modifications to one
subsystem is likely to have impact on the other. A desirable property of a subsystem decomposition
is that subsystems are as loosely coupled as possible. This minimizes the impact that errors or
future changes have on the correct operation of the system.

 Function points allow the measurement of software size in standard units, independent of
the underlying language in which the software is developed.
 Counting the number of externals (inputs, outputs, inquiries, and interfaces) that make up
the system.
 There are five types of externals to count:
1. External inputs - data or control inputs (input files, tables, forms, screens, messages,
etc.) to the system
2. External outputs - data or control outputs from the system
3. External inquiries - I/O queries which require a response (prompts, interrupts, calls,
etc.)
4. External interfaces - libraries or programs which are passed into and out of the system
(I/O routines, sorting procedures, math libraries, run-time libraries, etc.)
5. Internal data files - groupings of data stored internally in the system (entities, internal
control files, directories)
Apply these steps to calculate the size of a project:
1. Count or estimate all the occurrences of each type of external.
2. Assign each occurrence a complexity weight.
3. Multiply each occurrence by its complexity weight, and total the results to obtain a
function count. Complexity weights are as listed below.

The stem quotes that principle's central idea: support extension while keeping established code stable. DRY, KISS and YAGNI address other concerns. module_refs.title: Software Engineering module
module_refs.quote:
5.1.4. Generalization
Generalization enables us to organize concepts in to hierarchies. There may be any number of
intermediate levels in between, covering more-or-less generalized concepts (e.g., Low Priority
Incident, Emergency, Disaster). Such hierarchies allow us to refer to many concepts precisely. When
we use the term Incident, we mean all instances of all types of Incidents. When we use the term
Emergency, we only refer to an Incident that requires an immediate response. This view of
generalization stems from modeling.
In an object-oriented programming language, inheritance is a reusability technique. If a class Child
inherits from a class Parent, all the attributes and methods available on Parent are automatically
available on Child. The class Child may add additional methods or override inherited methods,
thus refining the class Parent. As in the case of generalization, the class at the top of the hierarchy
tends to be the most general one, whereas the leaves tend to be the most specialized.

module_refs.title: Software Engineering module
module_refs.quote:
A class in an object-oriented system carefully delineates between its interfaces the routines and
attributes within a class are held together tightly. In a properly designed system, the classes will
be grouped into subsystems but remain independent; therefore, changing one class has no impact
on other classes, and so, the impact is minimized. However, the object-oriented approach is not a
panacea; nothing is magical here that will promote perfect design or perfect code.
Promotion of reusability
Objects are reusable because they are modeled directly out of a real-world problem domain. Each
object stands by itself or within a small circle of peers (other objects). Within this framework, the
class does not concern itself with the rest of the system or how it is going to be used within a
particular system.

Classes and objects
Class diagrams describe the structure of the system in terms of classes and objects. Classes are
abstractions that specify the attributes and behavior of a set of objects. Objects are entities that
encapsulate state and behavior. Each object has an identity: It can be referred individually and is
distinguishable from other objects.
In UML, classes and objects are depicted by boxes including three compartments. The top
compartment displays the name of the class or object. The center compartment displays its
attributes, and the bottom compartment displays its operations. The attribute and operation
compartment can be omitted for clarity. Object names are underlined to indicate that they are
instances. By convention, class names start with an uppercase letter. Objects in object diagrams

questions.stem: Customer representatives stay in close contact with developers and use feedback to reshape the next timeboxed work. Which methodology makes this collaboration and adaptation a foundational priority?

answer.explanation: Frequent stakeholder communication alone is possible in several lifecycles. The scenario additionally gives customer representatives ongoing access to the team and lets feedback reshape the next timeboxed body of work, matching Agile’s collaboration and adaptation values. Waterfall and the V-model primarily organize planned stages, while spiral organizes commitments around risk reduction. The combination of priorities, rather than communication frequency by itself, identifies the intended methodology.

choices.label: B

The latter still have value. Agile does not mean no planning or no documentation. A user story states a small user need and value, supported by acceptance criteria; an epic groups broader work.

Classical waterfall separates planned phases with reviewed deliverables. It fits well-understood, stable requirements and familiar technology; late feedback makes changes costly. module_refs.title: Software Engineering module
module_refs.quote:
3.4.2. Negotiating specifications with clients: Joint Application Design
Joint Application Design (JAD) is effectiveness lies in that the requirements elicitation work is
done in one single workshop session in which all stakeholders participate. Users, clients,
developers, and a trained session leader sit together in one room to present their viewpoint, listen
to other viewpoints, negotiate, and agree on a mutually acceptable solution. The outcome of the
workshop, the final JAD document, is a complete system specification document that includes
definitions of data elements, work flows, and interface screens. Because the final document is
jointly developed by the stakeholders (that is, the participants who not only have an interest in the
success of the project, but also can make substantial decisions) the final JAD document represents
an agreement between users, clients, and developers, and thus minimizes requirements changes
later in the development process.

answer.explanation: A use-case description captures an actor’s goal together with preconditions, main flow, alternatives and postconditions. This provides the structured behavioral requirements record in the scenario. Storyboards illustrate moments in an interaction and wireframes sketch interface structure; either can help discovery without supplying that full behavioral contract. Pair programming organizes two people’s implementation work. It is therefore use-case modeling that directly names the requested requirements representation.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Use-case modeling records actors, goals and structured successful and alternative flows.

choices.label: B

choices.label: C

evidence.quote: An actor is an external role interacting with the system; it can be a person, device or another system. A person may play several roles, and several people may play one role. A primary actor seeks a goal; a supporting actor provides a service. Ask which user groups perform main functions, administer or maintain the system, and which external systems exchange information.

A storyboard sketches a sequence of moments in a proposed interaction, helping people explore how a concept would be used. A wireframe sketches interface structure and the arrangement of content or controls. Both can inform requirements, but neither automatically supplies a complete use-case description with actors, preconditions, flows and postconditions.

Pair programming is a way for two programmers to work together on the same implementation task, commonly sharing a workstation with complementary writing and reviewing roles. It is an implementation collaboration practice rather than a replacement for modeling a user goal.

module_refs.title: Software Engineering module
module_refs.quote:
Actors are external entities that interact with the system. Examples of actors include a user role
(e.g., a system administrator, a bank customer, a bank teller) or another system (e.g., a central
database, a fabrication line). Actors have unique names and descriptions.
Use cases describe the behavior of the system as seen from an actor’s point of view. Behavior
described by the use case model is also called external behavior. A use case describes a function
provided by the system as a set of events that yields a visible result for the actors. Actors initiate a
use case to access the system functionality. The use case can then initiate other use cases and gather
more information from the actors. When actors and use cases exchange information, they are said
to communicate. We will see later that we represent these exchanges with communication
relationships.

module_refs.title: Software Engineering module
module_refs.quote:
To describe a use case, we use a template composed of six fields (see also Figure 2.2):
• The name of the use case is unique across the system so that developers (and project
participants) can unambiguously refer to the use case.
• Participating actors are actors interacting with the use case.
• Entry conditions describe the conditions that need to be satisfied before the use case is
initiated.
• The flow of events describes the sequence of actions of the use case, which are be
numbered for reference. The common case (i.e., cases that occur frequently) and the
exceptional cases (i.e., cases that seldom occur, such as errors and unusual conditions) are
described separately in different use cases for clarity.
• Exit conditions describe the conditions that are satisfied after the completion of the use
case.
• Special requirements are requirements that are not related to the functionality of the
system. These include constraints on the performance of the system, its implementation,
the hardware platforms it runs on, and so on.

module_refs.quote:
Client/server architecture
In the client/server architecture (Figure 6.9), a subsystem, the server, provides servicesto instances
of other subsystems called the clients, which are responsible for interacting with theuser. The
request for a service is usually done via a remote procedure call mechanism or acommon object
broker (e.g., CORBA or Java RMI). Control flow in the clients and the servers isindependent
except for synchronization to manage requests or to receive results.
Figure 6.9 Client/server architecture (UML class diagram).
Clients request services from one or more servers. The server has no knowledge of the client. The
client/server architecture is a generalization of the repository architecture.

module_refs.quote:
6.1.2. Services and subsystem interfaces
A subsystem is characterized by the services it provides to other subsystems. A service is a set of
related operations that share a common purpose. A subsystem providing a notification service, for
example, defines operations to send notices, look up notification channels, and subscribe and
unsubscribe to a channel.
The set of operations of a subsystem that are available to other subsystems form the subsystem
interface. The subsystem interface, also referred to as the application programmer interface (API),
includes the name of the operations, their parameters, their types, and their return values. System
design focuses on defining the services provided by each subsystem that is, enumerating the
operations, their parameters, and their high-level behavior. Object design will focus on defining
the subsystem interfaces, that is, the type of the parameters and the return value of each operation.
The definition of a subsystem in terms of the services it provides helps us focus on its interface as
opposed to its implementation. A good subsystem interface should provide as little information

module_refs.title: Software Engineering module
module_refs.quote:
Requirement’s elicitation focuses on describing the purpose of the system. The client, the
developers, and the users identify a problem area and define a system that addresses the problem.
Such a definition is called a system specification and serves as a contract between the client and
the developers. The system specification is structured and formalized during analysis to produce
an analysis model (see Figure 3.1). Both system specification and analysis model represent the
same information. They differ only in the language and notation they use. The system specification
is written in natural language, whereas the analysis model is usually expressed in a formal or
semiformal notation.

module_refs.title: Software Engineering module
module_refs.quote:
Analysis focuses on producing a model of the system, called the analysis model, which is correct,
complete, consistent, and verifiable. Analysis is different from requirements elicitation in that
developers focus on structuring and formalizing the requirements elicited from users
Figure 4.1 Products of requirements elicitation and analysis (UML activity diagram).
Althoughtheanalysismodelmaynotbeunderstandabletotheusersandtheclient, it helps developers
verify the system specification produced during requirements elicitation. There is a natural
tendency for users and developers to postpone difficult decisions until later in the project. A
decision may be difficult because of lack of domain knowledge, lack of technological knowledge,
or simply because of disagreements among users and developers. Postponing decisions enables the
project to move on smoothly and avoid confrontation with reality or peers. Unfortunately, difficult
decisions will eventually need to be made, often at higher cost when intrinsic problems are
discovered during testing, or worse, during user evaluation. Translating a system specification in
to a formal or semi-formal model forces developers to identify and resolve difficult issues early in
the development.

System and software design: The systems design process allocates the requirements to either

questions.stem: A team separates a reusable reporting component behind a stable interface so other applications can use it and its implementation can change without rewriting clients. Which benefit most directly captures both goals?

options.label: A
options.text: To improve the readability of the code

options.label: C
options.text: To facilitate code reuse and maintenance

options.label: D
options.text: To minimize the number of software defects

questions.hint: Separate responsibilities inside a component from dependencies across boundaries. Evaluate the stated structure, change and reuse goals without assuming guaranteed benefits.
sources: Computer Science MCQ practice collection · Question 24

answer.text: To facilitate code reuse and maintenance
answer.explanation: A module with a stable interface can be reused in another application, and hiding its implementation allows localized changes without rewriting its clients. Those are reuse and maintenance benefits. Readability may improve as well, but it does not fully describe the two goals stated in the scenario. Modularization does not automatically optimize memory use or eliminate defects; good boundaries and verification still matter.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Readability may improve, but it does not fully describe reuse across applications and localized change.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Memory efficiency is not guaranteed by separating modules.

choices.label: C

choices.label: D

evidence.quote: Logical cohesion groups similar-category operations, often selected by a flag; temporal cohesion groups operations done at the same time; functional cohesion focuses on one task. Splitting an unrelated three-purpose component improves modularity. If behavior is preserved, the restructuring is refactoring; the words are not mutually exclusive answers. Smaller modules can aid understanding, independent work, reuse and maintenance, but too many interfaces also create complexity.

module_refs.title: Software Engineering module
module_refs.quote:
6.1.1. Subsystems and classes
In order to reduce the complexity of the application domain, we identified smaller parts called
classes and organized them into packages. Similarly, to reduce the complexity of the solution
domain, we decompose a system into simpler parts, called subsystems, which are made of a
number of solution domain classes. In the case of complex subsystems, we recursively apply this
principle and decompose a subsystem into simpler subsystems (see Figure 6.2).

module_refs.title: Software Engineering module
module_refs.quote:
A class in an object-oriented system carefully delineates between its interfaces the routines and
attributes within a class are held together tightly. In a properly designed system, the classes will
be grouped into subsystems but remain independent; therefore, changing one class has no impact
on other classes, and so, the impact is minimized. However, the object-oriented approach is not a
panacea; nothing is magical here that will promote perfect design or perfect code.
Promotion of reusability
Objects are reusable because they are modeled directly out of a real-world problem domain. Each
object stands by itself or within a small circle of peers (other objects). Within this framework, the
class does not concern itself with the rest of the system or how it is going to be used within a
particular system.

module_refs.title: Software Engineering module
module_refs.quote:
6.1.3. Coupling and coherence
Coupling is the strength of dependencies between two subsystems. If two subsystems are loosely
coupled, they are relatively independent, and thus, modifications to one of the subsystems will
have little impact on the other. If two subsystems are strongly coupled, modifications to one
subsystem is likely to have impact on the other. A desirable property of a subsystem decomposition
is that subsystems are as loosely coupled as possible. This minimizes the impact that errors or
future changes have on the correct operation of the system.

questions.stem:
Which type of testing aims to uncover defects in the interaction between different components
of a software system?
questions.hint: Separate testing scope, technique and purpose. Use the stated workload, observable result or coverage target rather than a universal ranking.
sources: Computer Science MCQ practice collection · Question 25

answer.explanation: The defects sought are in communication or interfaces among combined components, so the applicable level is integration testing. Unit tests concentrate on isolated units and system tests assess the complete product. Regression testing instead describes checking for unintended effects after a change, and can include unit, integration or system tests. The distinction is between the scope of combination and the purpose that triggers a test run.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Unit testing concentrates on an isolated function or small component.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Integration testing targets interactions among combined parts.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: System testing checks the whole integrated system against requirements.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Regression is an after-change objective that can occur at several testing levels.

evidence.quote: Unit testing isolates a function, class or small component, often replacing dependencies with stubs/mocks; a driver invokes the unit and a stub substitutes a called dependency. Integration testing exercises interfaces and interactions among combined parts. System testing checks the complete integrated system against functional and nonfunctional requirements in a representative environment.

Functional tests check required behavior against the SRS and acceptance criteria. Performance tests assess speed, throughput and resources under a specified workload; load uses expected demands and stress exceeds normal limits. Usability, security, compatibility and reliability tests target their respective qualities. “Normal operating conditions” alone does not distinguish functional from performance testing.

questions.stem: Which programming paradigm is based on the concept of objects and their interactions?
questions.hint: Identify whether the scenario prioritizes delivery, learning, adaptation or risk reduction. Several processes can share individual practices, so compare their defining emphasis.
sources: Computer Science MCQ practice collection · Question 26

answer.explanation: Object-oriented programming organizes a system around objects that combine state and behavior and interact through operations. Procedural programming decomposes work into functions or procedures that manipulate data. Functional programming emphasizes function evaluation and controlled side effects, while event-driven programming organizes reactions to events. An object-oriented program may also use events or functions, but the question asks which paradigm is defined by objects and their interactions.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Functional programming emphasizes evaluation of functions and controlled side effects.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Procedural programming emphasizes functions or procedures operating on data.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Object-oriented programming centers on objects with state and behavior.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Event-driven programming centers on reactions to events, independent of object-based decomposition.

evidence.quote: Procedural decomposition organizes functions; object oriented decomposition organizes objects with state and behavior. Either can use iterative or sequential development. OOP does not automatically shorten every project. Reuse, encapsulation and consistent models can reduce duplication and ease change; poor object design can still be complex. Functional programming emphasizes function evaluation and controlled side effects; event-driven programs react to events.

questions.stem: What is the defining artifact-management function of version control, distinguishing it from collaboration benefits and CI services?

options.label: A
options.text: To manage project schedules and milestones

options.label: B
options.text: To facilitate collaboration among team members

options.label: C
options.text: To track and control changes to source code and files

options.label: D
options.text: To automate the testing and deployment processes

questions.hint: Separate artifact history and controlled changes from scheduling, collaboration benefits and automated execution.
sources: Computer Science MCQ practice collection · Question 27

answer.text: To track and control changes to source code and files
answer.explanation: Version control records artifact versions and their history, making it possible to inspect changes, maintain branches and combine compatible work. Collaboration is an important benefit, but it is broader than the defining version-history function. Scheduling belongs to project planning, while automated testing and deployment belong to CI or delivery tooling that can use version-control events. These roles can be integrated without becoming the same activity.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Scheduling and milestones belong to project planning and tracking.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Collaboration is a benefit enabled by shared versions and merging, rather than the defining artifact-history function.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Tracking and controlling file changes is the direct version-control function.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Testing and deployment automation is CI/delivery work that may integrate with version control.

evidence.quote: Configuration management identifies controlled items, versions/baselines, change procedures, status and audits. Items may include source code, requirements, manuals, test plans, environments and build configurations. A team’s ordinary browser is usually a tool rather than product CI, but a controlled test-browser version may be an environment CI.
Git tracks versions; issue trackers such as Jira track work/defects; CI tools such as Jenkins automate checks; Docker packages application/runtime dependencies into containers.

module_refs.title: Software Engineering module
module_refs.quote:
Configuration management avoids faults caused by undisciplined change in the system models.
For example, it is a common mistake to a change a subsystem interface without notifying all
developers of calling components. Configuration management can make sure that, if analysis
models and code are becoming inconsistent with one another, analysts and implementor are
notified. The assumption behind configuration management is that the system contains many less
faults if change is controlled.

questions.stem: Which conventional lifecycle is described by a simple linear requirements→design→implementation→testing sequence with reviewed phase completion, without the V-model’s explicit development-to-test pairing?
questions.hint: Identify whether the scenario prioritizes delivery, learning, adaptation or risk reduction. Several processes can share individual practices, so compare their defining emphasis.
sources: Computer Science MCQ practice collection · Question 28

answer.explanation: Classical waterfall organizes work as separated planned phases with reviewed deliverables, matching the stated linear sequence. The V-model additionally pairs development artifacts with later test levels, which this question excludes. Agile emphasizes adaptation and feedback, while spiral organizes repeated risk-driven cycles. Explicitly distinguishing the test-pairing structure removes the overlap between two staged processes without denying their relationship.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Classical waterfall matches the specified simple linear organization.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Agile emphasizes adaptive content and feedback.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Spiral uses risk-driven cycles.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: The V-model adds explicit development-to-test pairing excluded here.

evidence.quote: The V-model pairs specification/design stages with later test levels. Requirements inform acceptance tests; system design informs system tests; component/detail design informs integration/unit tests. Coding lies at the bottom. Test planning starts early. Stable requirements and strong assurance may favor this organization, but neither a V shape nor waterfall guarantees safety or correctness.
Classical waterfall separates planned phases with reviewed deliverables. It fits well-understood, stable requirements and familiar technology; late feedback makes changes costly.

module_refs.quote:

a waterfall) through the development phases. Thus the waterfall model maintains that one should
move to a phase only when its preceding phase is reviewed and verified. That is, each phase must
be completed before the next phase can begin. In waterfall model phases do not overlap. But there

questions.stem: What is the primary purpose of software documentation?

options.label: A
options.text: To serve as a record of code authorship

options.label: C
options.text: To assist in software maintenance and understanding

options.label: D
options.text: To ensure compliance with coding standards

questions.hint: Distinguish process assurance from product evaluation, and compare specified obligations with actual stakeholder needs.
sources: Computer Science MCQ practice collection · Question 29

answer.text: To assist in software maintenance and understanding
answer.explanation: Documentation records requirements and architecture so developers can understand decisions, revisit designs and coordinate later change. A user manual is one audience-specific part of this broader purpose.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Authorship alone does not capture system decisions or behavior. See PDF p. 130, 83, 32.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: End-user instructions are a valid subset, not the overall technical purpose. See PDF p. 130, 83, 32.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Matches understanding, revisiting and maintaining documented structures. See PDF p. 130, 83, 32.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Coding-standard compliance is narrower than the general understanding purpose. See PDF p. 130, 83, 32.

evidence.quote: Quality assurance establishes and checks processes/standards; quality control evaluates work products. An SQA plan identifies standards, responsibilities, evaluations, reviews, audits and assurance records. Quality of conformance means following the design/specification; a product can conform to a poor specification. Verification asks whether specified obligations are implemented correctly; validation asks whether the product meets intended stakeholder needs. Both can use reviews, analysis or execution, so “human-only versus computer-only” is false.

module_refs.title: Software Engineering module
module_refs.quote:
6.3. DOCUMENTING SYSTEM DESIGN
System design is documented in the System Design Document (SDD). It describes design goals
set by the project, the subsystem decomposition (with UML class diagrams), the
hardware/software mapping (with UML deployment diagrams), the data management, the access
control, control flow mechanisms, and boundary conditions. The SDD is used to define interfaces
between teams of developers and as reference when architecture-level decisions need to be
revisited. The audience for the SDD includes the project management, the system architects (i.e.,
the developers who participate in the system design), and the developers who design and
implement each subsystem. The following is an example template for a SDD:

module_refs.title: Software Engineering module
module_refs.quote:
3.4.4. Documenting Requirements Elicitation
The results of the requirements elicitation activity and the analysis activity are documented in the
Requirements Analysis Document (RAD). This document completely describes the system in
terms of functional and nonfunctional requirements and serves as a contractual basis between the
client and the developers. The audience for the RAD includes the client, the users, the project
management, the system analysts (i.e., the developers who participate in the requirements), and
the system designers (i.e., the developers who participate in the system design). The first part of
the document, including use cases and nonfunctional requirements, is written during requirements
elicitation. The formalization of the specification in terms of object models is written during
analysis.
The first section of the RAD is an Introduction. Its purpose is to provide a brief overview of the
function of the system and the reasons for its development, its scope, and references to the
development context (e.g., related problem statement, references to existing systems, feasibility
studies). The introduction also includes the objectives and success criteria of the project.

questions.stem: After each short usable release, customers reorder the remaining work and the team adapts the next release’s content while keeping its timebox. Which broad approach most directly fits this planning behavior?
questions.hint: Identify whether the scenario prioritizes delivery, learning, adaptation or risk reduction. Several processes can share individual practices, so compare their defining emphasis.
sources: Computer Science MCQ practice collection · Question 30

answer.explanation: A fixed short timebox with usable results and customer-driven adaptation of later content fits Agile planning. Classical waterfall and the V-model organize planned development stages, with the latter pairing stages to tests. Spiral cycles organize commitments around risk assessment and reduction. All can incorporate some staged work, so the stated treatment of feedback and later scope is what makes the Agile option the most direct match.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Classical waterfall emphasizes planned phases and later delivery feedback.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Agile adapts later work from customer feedback while producing usable increments.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Spiral is specifically organized around risk reduction, not the stated timeboxed adaptation rule.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: The V-model is defined by paired development and test stages.

evidence.quote: Choose incremental delivery when prioritized partial capability must reach users early. Smaller changes can be easier to debug and permit feedback, though architecture and integration still require planning. Iteration need not rebuild the whole system every time, and increments need not be perfectly independent modules. Broad descriptions of early working software can fit prototypes, iterative or Agile processes; identify the purpose of that early version.

Classical waterfall separates planned phases with reviewed deliverables. It fits well-understood, stable requirements and familiar technology; late feedback makes changes costly. It does not make change physically impossible: real projects revisit work under control, and modified waterfall explicitly includes feedback. Rigidity offers milestone visibility but can freeze incorrect assumptions.

Spiral development is risk driven. Each cycle identifies objectives and alternatives, assesses and reduces important risks, develops/verifies an appropriate next result, and plans further commitment. A prototype may test a risky technology before a large investment. The amount and type of work depend on the risks.

Scrum uses timeboxed Sprints of at most one month, with a Sprint Goal, selected work and a usable Increment meeting a Definition of Done. Scope is discussed before and during planning; it is not forbidden to agree scope. Timeboxes tend to stay fixed while content is adapted without endangering the goal. Agile can be combined with required assurance/documentation; safety-critical context alone cannot prove it is unsuitable.

module_refs.title: Software Engineering module
module_refs.quote:
This model delivers software in small but usable pieces, called ―increments. In general, each
increment builds on those that have already been delivered. The model is iterative in nature and
focuses on the delivery of an operational product with each increment. Early increments are
stripped down versions of the final product, but they do provide capability that serves the user and
also provide a platform for evaluation by the user.

module_refs.title: Software Engineering module
module_refs.quote:
Sometimes, software processes are categorized as either plan-driven or agile processes. Plan-
driven processes are processes where all of the process activities are planned in advance and
progress is measured against this plan. In agile processes planning is incremental and it is easier
to change the process to reflect changing customer requirements. There is no hard and fast rules to
follow but each approach is suitable for different types of software. Generally, you need to find a
balance between plan-driven and agile processes.

questions.stem:
Which design principle advocates for designing software components that have a single
responsibility?
questions.hint: Separate responsibilities inside a component from dependencies across boundaries. Evaluate the stated structure, change and reuse goals without assuming guaranteed benefits.
sources: Computer Science MCQ practice collection · Question 31

answer.explanation: SE25 identifies Single Responsibility among the core design principles. The question asks directly for one responsibility per component, so D is the exact named rule. Encapsulation protects internal decisions, inheritance creates subtype relations, and polymorphism supports varying implementations through a common interface. Those can help a design but do not themselves define a single responsibility.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Encapsulation hides implementation details rather than requiring one responsibility per component.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Inheritance establishes superclass/subclass reuse rather than the focused-responsibility rule.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Polymorphism supports compatible varying implementations rather than defining responsibility count.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Single Responsibility explicitly calls for one focused responsibility in a software component.

evidence.quote: SOLID includes Single Responsibility, Open–Closed, Liskov substitution, Interface Segregation and Dependency Inversion.

Generalization places common concepts in a more general superclass and specialized concepts in subclasses. Available inherited attributes and operations are shared by subclasses, which may extend or override behavior.

Encapsulation groups state with operations and hides representation behind an interface. Polymorphism permits different object types to respond differently through a common operation or interface. Abstraction exposes the relevant contract while omitting unnecessary detail. Reusability means using suitable existing classes or components in new contexts rather than writing them again. These ideas support each other but name different properties.

module_refs.title: Software Engineering module
module_refs.quote:
Coherence is the strength of dependencies within a subsystem. If a subsystem contains many
objects that are related to each other and perform similar tasks, its coherence is high. If a subsystem
contains a number of unrelated objects, its coherence is low. A desirable property of a subsystem
decomposition is that it leads to subsystems with high coherence.

module_refs.title: Software Engineering module
module_refs.quote:
The analysis object model consists of entity, boundary, and control objects. Entity objects
represent the persistent information tracked by the system. Boundary objects represent the
interactions between the actors and the system. Control objects represent the tasks that a formed
by the user and supported by the system. In the 2B watch example, Year, Month, Day are entity
objects; Button Boundary and LCD Display Boundary are boundary objects; Change Date Control is
a control object that represents the activity of changing the date by pressing combinations of
buttons.

questions.stem:
Which design pattern is used to ensure that only one instance of a class is created throughout
the system?
questions.hint: Separate responsibilities inside a component from dependencies across boundaries. Evaluate the stated structure, change and reuse goals without assuming guaranteed benefits.
sources: Computer Science MCQ practice collection · Question 32

answer.explanation: SE27 describes Singleton as controlling access to one instance. That is the pattern requested by the one-instance condition. Factory patterns address how concrete objects are created, Observer notifies subscribers and Decorator adds behavior by wrapping. None of those other pattern responsibilities guarantees a single shared instance by itself.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Singleton controls creation and access so that the intended class has one shared instance.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: A factory selects or constructs products rather than inherently limiting a class to one instance.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Observer distributes notifications to subscribers rather than restricting object instance count.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Decorator adds behavior through wrapping rather than enforcing a single instance.

evidence.quote: Factory Method lets subclasses choose a concrete product through a creation operation, reducing coupling to concrete constructors. A simple factory centralizes creation but is not identical to Factory Method. Singleton controls access to one instance; Observer notifies subscribers; Memento stores/restores state while hiding representation; Iterator traverses; Decorator adds behavior through wrapping. The pattern name is Memento, not Momento.

module_refs.title: Software Engineering module
module_refs.quote:
6.1.4. Software architecture
As the complexity of systems increases, the specification of the system decomposition is critical.
It is difficult to modify or correct a weak decomposition once development has started, as most
subsystem interfaces have to change. In recognition of the importance of this problem, the concept
of software architecture has emerged. A software architecture includes the system
decomposition, the global control flow, error-handling policies and inter subsystem
communication protocols.
In this section, we describe a few sample architectures that can be used for different systems. This
is by no means a systematic or thorough exposition of the subject. Rather, we aim to provide a few
representative examples and refer the reader to the literature for more details.

questions.hint: Identify whether the scenario prioritizes delivery, learning, adaptation or risk reduction. Several processes can share individual practices, so compare their defining emphasis.

answer.text: Functional programming, for the side-effect emphasis.
answer.explanation: The phrase promotes the use of data is not distinctive because all these paradigms use data. The discriminating part is avoiding or controlling side effects. SE01 explicitly assigns function evaluation and controlled side effects to functional programming. Procedural, object-oriented and event-driven styles organize behavior differently and do not inherently impose that emphasis.

questions.stem:
Which type of software maintenance involves making changes to a software system to adapt
it to new environments or technologies?
questions.hint: Classify the motive for the change before its implementation: repair, environment, useful capability or reduced future risk.
sources: Computer Science MCQ practice collection · Question 35

answer.explanation: SE40 defines adaptive maintenance as responding to changes in the environment. New platforms or technologies therefore create an adaptive-maintenance need even when the original software is not faulty. Corrective maintenance fixes faults, perfective work improves useful capability or performance, and preventive work reduces future risk. The stated environmental motive makes B the appropriate category.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Corrective work fixes faults rather than primarily accommodating changed environments or technology.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Adaptive maintenance changes software so it continues working in a new environment or technology context.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Perfective work improves capability or performance rather than specifically responding to an environmental change.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Preventive work reduces future maintenance risk rather than defining adaptation to a new environment.

evidence.quote: Corrective maintenance fixes faults; adaptive maintenance responds to environment changes; perfective maintenance improves useful capability/performance; preventive maintenance reduces future risk, such as restructuring fragile code. Motive determines category; refactoring can support preventive or perfective work. Maintenance often lasts years and includes understanding legacy code and regression effort, so it may dominate lifecycle cost.

module_refs.title: Software Engineering module
module_refs.quote:
5. Operation and maintenance: Normally (although not necessarily), this is the longest life cycle
phase. Maintenance of a typical software product requires much more than the effort necessary to
develop the product itself. The system is installed and put into practical use. Maintenance involves
correcting errors which were not discovered in earlier stages of the life cycle, improving the
implementation of system units and enhancing the system ‘s services as new requirements are
discovered.

module_refs.quote:
✓ Software evolution takes place when you change existing software systems to meet new
requirements. Changes are continuous and the software must evolve to remain useful.

answer.text: To assess the user-friendliness and ease of use of the software system

module_refs.quote:
though this type of approach could be used for any parameter, usability tests focus on usability
parameters, such as the ease to learn the system, the time to accomplish a task, or the rate of errors
a user makes when accomplishing a task.
There are two important differences between classical experiments and usability tests. Whereas
the classical experimental method is designed to confirm or refute a hypothesis, the goal of
usability tests is to obtain qualitative information on how to fix usability problems and how to
improve the system. Another difference is the rigor with which the experiments need to be
performed. It has been shown that even a series of quick focused tests starting as early as
requirements elicitation is extremely helpful. Nielsen uses the term “discount usability
engineering” to indicate that a few usability tests are better than none at all.

Which software development methodology involves iterative development cycles called
sprints?
questions.hint: Identify whether the scenario prioritizes delivery, learning, adaptation or risk reduction. Several processes can share individual practices, so compare their defining emphasis.
sources: Computer Science MCQ practice collection · Question 37

answer.explanation: SE05 places Sprints in Scrum, an Agile framework. B is therefore the available category that contains the specific process described. Agile as a whole does not require every method to call its iterations Sprints. Waterfall, spiral and the V-model have other organizing principles, so none is the named Sprint-based method.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Classical waterfall uses planned phases rather than Scrum Sprints.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Scrum is an Agile framework whose iterative delivery cycles are called Sprints.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Spiral uses risk-driven cycles rather than specifically the Scrum Sprint mechanism.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: The V-model pairs development stages with tests rather than organizing work into Sprints.

evidence.quote: Scrum uses timeboxed Sprints of at most one month, with a Sprint Goal, selected work and a usable Increment meeting a Definition of Done. Scope is discussed before and during planning; it is not forbidden to agree scope. Timeboxes tend to stay fixed while content is adapted without endangering the goal. Agile can be combined with required assurance/documentation; safety-critical context alone cannot prove it is unsuitable.

module_refs.quote:
Sometimes, software processes are categorized as either plan-driven or agile processes. Plan-

progress is measured against this plan. In agile processes planning is incremental and it is easier
to change the process to reflect changing customer requirements. There is no hard and fast rules to
follow but each approach is suitable for different types of software. Generally, you need to find a
balance between plan-driven and agile processes.

answer.text: To improve the readability and maintainability of the code

questions.stem: Which approach treats customer participation in reviewing working results and reprioritizing future work as a foundational value, rather than merely a practice a project may choose?
questions.hint: Identify whether the scenario prioritizes delivery, learning, adaptation or risk reduction. Several processes can share individual practices, so compare their defining emphasis.
sources: Computer Science MCQ practice collection · Question 39

answer.explanation: The project treats customer participation in reviewing results and reprioritizing future work as a foundational development value. This directly matches Agile’s customer collaboration and responsiveness to change. Waterfall and the V-model primarily define phase and test-stage organization. Spiral also includes stakeholder review, but risk assessment and reduction define its cycle. Participation alone is not exclusive; the explicit priority given to continual adaptive collaboration identifies the answer.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Classical waterfall’s defining organization is planned phase progression.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Agile explicitly prioritizes customer collaboration and adapting to feedback.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Spiral includes review but is defined by risk-driven cycles.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: The V-model organizes linked development and test stages, rather than naming the stated collaboration values.

evidence.quote: Agile favors people collaborating, useful working results, customer participation and adaptation over rigid adherence to procedures, exhaustive documents, contracts or fixed plans. The latter still have value. Agile does not mean no planning or no documentation. A user story states a small user need and value, supported by acceptance criteria; an epic groups broader work.

Classical waterfall separates planned phases with reviewed deliverables. It fits well-understood, stable requirements and familiar technology; late feedback makes changes costly. It does not make change physically impossible: real projects revisit work under control, and modified waterfall explicitly includes feedback. Rigidity offers milestone visibility but can freeze incorrect assumptions.

Spiral development is risk driven. Each cycle identifies objectives and alternatives, assesses and reduces important risks, develops/verifies an appropriate next result, and plans further commitment. A prototype may test a risky technology before a large investment. The amount and type of work depend on the risks.

module_refs.title: Software Engineering module
module_refs.quote:
3.4.2. Negotiating specifications with clients: Joint Application Design
Joint Application Design (JAD) is effectiveness lies in that the requirements elicitation work is
done in one single workshop session in which all stakeholders participate. Users, clients,
developers, and a trained session leader sit together in one room to present their viewpoint, listen
to other viewpoints, negotiate, and agree on a mutually acceptable solution. The outcome of the
workshop, the final JAD document, is a complete system specification document that includes
definitions of data elements, work flows, and interface screens. Because the final document is
jointly developed by the stakeholders (that is, the participants who not only have an interest in the
success of the project, but also can make substantial decisions) the final JAD document represents
an agreement between users, clients, and developers, and thus minimizes requirements changes
later in the development process.

questions.stem:
Which type of testing involves running the entire software system in an environment that
closely resembles the production environment?
questions.hint: Separate testing scope, technique and purpose. Use the stated workload, observable result or coverage target rather than a universal ranking.
sources: Computer Science MCQ practice collection · Question 40

answer.explanation: System testing evaluates the complete integrated software against its functional and nonfunctional requirements in a representative environment. Unit testing isolates a smaller element and integration testing concentrates on interfaces among combined parts. Regression testing instead checks for unintended consequences after change and is not restricted to any one level or environment. The question specifies the complete-product scope, making system testing the direct classification.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Unit testing isolates a function, class or small component.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Integration testing focuses on interfaces and interactions among combined parts.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: System testing evaluates the complete integrated product in a representative environment.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Regression names an after-change checking purpose and can run at multiple levels.

evidence.quote: Unit testing isolates a function, class or small component, often replacing dependencies with stubs/mocks; a driver invokes the unit and a stub substitutes a called dependency. Integration testing exercises interfaces and interactions among combined parts. System testing checks the complete integrated system against functional and nonfunctional requirements in a representative environment.

Functional tests check required behavior against the SRS and acceptance criteria. Performance tests assess speed, throughput and resources under a specified workload; load uses expected demands and stress exceeds normal limits. Usability, security, compatibility and reliability tests target their respective qualities. “Normal operating conditions” alone does not distinguish functional from performance testing.

options.label: A
options.text: A description of a specific user interface design

options.label: B
options.text: A step-by-step procedure for software installation

options.label: C

options.label: D

questions.hint: Match the information to be represented with each model’s purpose. Read relationship direction, boundary and ownership conditions before classifying it.

answer.text: A sequence of activities performed by a user or system
answer.explanation: A use case describes a system-provided function as a flow of events producing an actor-visible result. C is acceptable when understood as goal-related interactions, not any arbitrary sequence of activities.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: UI layout is an implementation/interface design artifact. See PDF p. 47, 48.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Installation instructions are one possible documented procedure, not the general use-case definition. See PDF p. 47, 48.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Best matches the goal-oriented flow of events involving actors and the system. See PDF p. 47, 48.

choices.label: D

The diagram shows roles, goals and relationships, not the full detailed algorithm or UI layout. module_refs.title: Software Engineering module
module_refs.quote:
Actors are external entities that interact with the system. Examples of actors include a user role
(e.g., a system administrator, a bank customer, a bank teller) or another system (e.g., a central
database, a fabrication line). Actors have unique names and descriptions.
Use cases describe the behavior of the system as seen from an actor’s point of view. Behavior
described by the use case model is also called external behavior. A use case describes a function
provided by the system as a set of events that yields a visible result for the actors. Actors initiate a
use case to access the system functionality. The use case can then initiate other use cases and gather
more information from the actors. When actors and use cases exchange information, they are said
to communicate. We will see later that we represent these exchanges with communication
relationships.

module_refs.title: Software Engineering module
module_refs.quote:
To describe a use case, we use a template composed of six fields (see also Figure 2.2):
• The name of the use case is unique across the system so that developers (and project
participants) can unambiguously refer to the use case.
• Participating actors are actors interacting with the use case.
• Entry conditions describe the conditions that need to be satisfied before the use case is
initiated.
• The flow of events describes the sequence of actions of the use case, which are be
numbered for reference. The common case (i.e., cases that occur frequently) and the
exceptional cases (i.e., cases that seldom occur, such as errors and unusual conditions) are
described separately in different use cases for clarity.
• Exit conditions describe the conditions that are satisfied after the completion of the use
case.
• Special requirements are requirements that are not related to the functionality of the
system. These include constraints on the performance of the system, its implementation,
the hardware platforms it runs on, and so on.

module_refs.title: Software Engineering module
module_refs.quote:
Extend relationships
Extend relationships are an alternate means for reducing complexity in the use case model. A use
case can extend another use case by adding events. An extend relationship indicates that an
instance of an extended use case may include (under certain conditions) the behavior specified by
the extending use case. A typical application of extend relationships is the specification of
exceptional behavior. For example (Figure 2-19), assume that the network connection between the
Dispatcher and the FieldOfficer can be interrupted at any time. (e.g., if the FieldOfficer enters a
tunnel). The use case ConnectionDown describes the set of events taken by the system and the
actors while the connection is lost. ConnectionDown extends the use cases OpenIncident and
AllocateResources. Separating exceptional behavior from common behavior enables us to write
shorter and more focused use cases.

questions.stem: What defines an abstract use case, rather than optionality, unfinished documentation or reuse alone?

Generalization relationships
Generalization/specialization relationships are a third mechanism for reducing the complexity of
a model. A use case can specialize a more general one by adding more detail. For example,

developers describe the Authenticate use case in more detail and allow for several different
hardware platforms. This refinement activity results in two more use cases,
AuthenticateWithPasswordwhich enables FieldOfficers to login without any specific hardware,
and AuthenticateWithCard, which enables FieldOfficers to login using a smart card. The two new
use cases are represented as specializations of the Authenticate use case.

questions.stem: Which option states the most specific defining purpose of an exception flow, distinguishing it from a generic alternative flow?

answer.text: To represent an error or exceptional situation in the use case
answer.explanation: An exception flow handles an error or failure encountered in the use case. Such a path is also an alternative to the main success flow in a broad sense, but B alone does not distinguish exceptional handling from normal conditional variations. An exception may allow correction and recovery instead of terminating the use case. Actor relationships do not define its failure-handling purpose.

choices.label: A

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Alternative path is broader and does not identify the exceptional nature.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Exceptions need not terminate the entire use case.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Actor relationships do not describe failure handling.

evidence.quote: Example: Submit Incident. Precondition: officer authenticated. 1 Officer supplies location and description. 2 System validates details. 3 System records the incident. 4 System returns its ID. Alternative 2a: location missing → report the problem and request correction; save nothing. Success postcondition: incident and ID persist; failure guarantee: no partial record. An alternate flow is a conditional variation; an exception flow handles a failure. Preconditions hold before entry, while a trigger starts the use case.

module_refs.title: Software Engineering module
module_refs.quote:
To describe a use case, we use a template composed of six fields (see also Figure 2.2):
• The name of the use case is unique across the system so that developers (and project
participants) can unambiguously refer to the use case.
• Participating actors are actors interacting with the use case.
• Entry conditions describe the conditions that need to be satisfied before the use case is
initiated.
• The flow of events describes the sequence of actions of the use case, which are be
numbered for reference. The common case (i.e., cases that occur frequently) and the
exceptional cases (i.e., cases that seldom occur, such as errors and unusual conditions) are
described separately in different use cases for clarity.
• Exit conditions describe the conditions that are satisfied after the completion of the use
case.
• Special requirements are requirements that are not related to the functionality of the
system. These include constraints on the performance of the system, its implementation,
the hardware platforms it runs on, and so on.

module_refs.title: Software Engineering module
module_refs.quote:
Extend relationships
Extend relationships are an alternate means for reducing complexity in the use case model. A use
case can extend another use case by adding events. An extend relationship indicates that an
instance of an extended use case may include (under certain conditions) the behavior specified by
the extending use case. A typical application of extend relationships is the specification of
exceptional behavior. For example (Figure 2-19), assume that the network connection between the
Dispatcher and the FieldOfficer can be interrupted at any time. (e.g., if the FieldOfficer enters a
tunnel). The use case ConnectionDown describes the set of events taken by the system and the
actors while the connection is lost. ConnectionDown extends the use cases OpenIncident and
AllocateResources. Separating exceptional behavior from common behavior enables us to write
shorter and more focused use cases.

questions.stem: What is the primary goal of use case modeling?

options.label: A
options.text: To define the software architecture of the system

options.label: B
options.text: To identify and document user requirements

options.label: C
options.text: To design the user interface of the system

options.label: D

answer.text: To identify and document user requirements
answer.explanation: Use cases capture externally visible functionality and let developers validate requirements with users, rather than defining internal architecture or implementation.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: System design defines architecture after the external analysis model. See PDF p. 47, 62.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Directly captures actor-visible functional requirements. See PDF p. 47, 62.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: UI layout can be explored alongside use cases but is not their primary purpose. See PDF p. 47, 62.

choices.label: D

evidence.quote: An actor is an external role interacting with the system; it can be a person, device or another system. A person may play several roles, and several people may play one role. A primary actor seeks a goal; a supporting actor provides a service. Ask which user groups perform main functions, administer or maintain the system, and which external systems exchange information.

module_refs.title: Software Engineering module
module_refs.quote:
Actors are external entities that interact with the system. Examples of actors include a user role
(e.g., a system administrator, a bank customer, a bank teller) or another system (e.g., a central
database, a fabrication line). Actors have unique names and descriptions.
Use cases describe the behavior of the system as seen from an actor’s point of view. Behavior
described by the use case model is also called external behavior. A use case describes a function
provided by the system as a set of events that yields a visible result for the actors. Actors initiate a
use case to access the system functionality. The use case can then initiate other use cases and gather
more information from the actors. When actors and use cases exchange information, they are said
to communicate. We will see later that we represent these exchanges with communication
relationships.

module_refs.title: Software Engineering module
module_refs.quote:
Requirement’s elicitation focuses on describing the purpose of the system. The client, the
developers, and the users identify a problem area and define a system that addresses the problem.
Such a definition is called a system specification and serves as a contract between the client and
the developers. The system specification is structured and formalized during analysis to produce
an analysis model (see Figure 3.1). Both system specification and analysis model represent the
same information. They differ only in the language and notation they use. The system specification
is written in natural language, whereas the analysis model is usually expressed in a formal or
semiformal notation.

questions.stem: What is an alternative flow in a use case?

options.label: A
options.text: A flowchart representation of the use case steps

options.label: B
options.text: A flow of activities that occurs in parallel with the main flow

options.label: C
options.text: A different sequence of steps based on specific conditions

options.label: D
options.text: A representation of the relationship between use cases

questions.hint: Match the information to be represented with each model’s purpose. Read relationship direction, boundary and ownership conditions before classifying it.
sources: Computer Science MCQ practice collection · Question 49

answer.text: A different sequence of steps based on specific conditions
answer.explanation: A flow of events describes interactions; exceptional conditions introduce alternative event sequences. This is a different path under a condition, rather than necessarily concurrency or inter-use-case structure.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: A flowchart is a representation format, not the alternative sequence itself. See PDF p. 48, 50.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Parallel execution is not required by an alternative branch. See PDF p. 48, 50.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Directly describes a condition-dependent event sequence. See PDF p. 48, 50.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Include/extend/generalization describe relationships, not the definition of every alternative flow. See PDF p. 48, 50.

evidence.quote: Example: Submit Incident. Precondition: officer authenticated. 1 Officer supplies location and description. 2 System validates details. 3 System records the incident. 4 System returns its ID. Alternative 2a: location missing → report the problem and request correction; save nothing. Success postcondition: incident and ID persist; failure guarantee: no partial record. An alternate flow is a conditional variation; an exception flow handles a failure. Preconditions hold before entry, while a trigger starts the use case.

questions.stem:
Identifying and describing the fundamental software system abstractions and their relationships.
Establishing the overall system architecture — in which phase are these activities done?
questions.hint: Separate responsibilities inside a component from dependencies across boundaries. Evaluate the stated structure, change and reuse goals without assuming guaranteed benefits.
sources: Computer Science Exit Exam practice collection · Question 7

answer.explanation: System and software design establish the overall architecture and identify software abstractions and relationships.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Direct match to the described design tasks. See PDF p. 18, 116.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Establishes required services, constraints and goals. See PDF p. 18, 116.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Checks complete-system behavior. See PDF p. 18, 116.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Translates a design into code. See PDF p. 18, 116.

evidence.quote: System design turns the analysis model into architecture: design goals, subsystem responsibilities, dependencies, hardware mapping, data management, access control, control flow and startup/shutdown/error policies. Detail/object design refines APIs, parameter/return types, exceptions, component choices and algorithms. A subsystem is a manageable logical collection with services and an interface; it need not be a physical replaceable artifact.

module_refs.title: Software Engineering module
module_refs.quote:
System and software design: The systems design process allocates the requirements to either
hardware or software systems by establishing an overall system architecture.
Software design involves identifying and describing the fundamental software system abstractions
and their relationships. The goal of the design phase is to transform the requirements specified in
the SRS document into a structure that is suitable for implementation in some programming
language. In technical terms, during the design phase the software architecture is derived from the
SRS document. Two distinctly different approaches are available: the traditional design approach
and the object-oriented design approach.

module_refs.title: Software Engineering module
module_refs.quote:
The analysis model describes the system completely from the actors’ point of view and serves as
the basis of communication between the client and the developers. The analysis model, however,
does not contain information about the internal structure of the system, its hardware configuration,
or, more generally, how the system should be realized. System design is the first step in this
direction. System design results in the following products:
• List of design goals, describing the qualities of the system that developers should optimize
• Software architecture, describing the subsystem decomposition in terms of subsystem
responsibilities, dependencies among subsystems, subsystem mapping to hardware, and
major policy decisions such as control flow, access control, and data storage.
The design goals are derived from the nonfunctional requirements. Design goals guide the
decisions to be made by the developers especially when trade-offs are needed. The subsystem
decomposition constitutes the bulk of system design. Developers divide the system into
manageable pieces to deal with complexity: Each subsystem is assigned to a team and realized
independently. In order for this to be possible, though, developers need to address system-wide

questions.stem:
Instead of delivering the system as a single delivery, development and delivery is broken down into
phases with each phase delivering part of the required functionality. What type of development model is this?
questions.hint: Identify whether the scenario prioritizes delivery, learning, adaptation or risk reduction. Several processes can share individual practices, so compare their defining emphasis.
sources: Computer Science Exit Exam practice collection · Question 8

answer.explanation: Successive deliveries that each add part of the required usable functionality define incremental development. The product gains capability across these deliveries rather than waiting for a single completed-system handoff. Waterfall and a generic linear model organize phase sequence. Spiral is organized around risk assessment, and evolutionary development broadly describes refinement. Those can overlap with staged delivery, but incremental is the specific name for the delivery organization stated.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Incremental development adds usable required functionality in successive deliveries.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Waterfall names planned phase progression, not this particular staged-capability strategy.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Spiral names risk-driven cycles, even when increments are produced.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Evolutionary refinement is broader than the specific addition-of-functionality strategy described.

evidence.quote: Choose incremental delivery when prioritized partial capability must reach users early. Smaller changes can be easier to debug and permit feedback, though architecture and integration still require planning. Iteration need not rebuild the whole system every time, and increments need not be perfectly independent modules. Broad descriptions of early working software can fit prototypes, iterative or Agile processes; identify the purpose of that early version.

Spiral development is risk driven. Each cycle identifies objectives and alternatives, assesses and reduces important risks, develops/verifies an appropriate next result, and plans further commitment. A prototype may test a risky technology before a large investment. The amount and type of work depend on the risks.

module_refs.title: Software Engineering module
module_refs.quote:
This model delivers software in small but usable pieces, called ―increments. In general, each
increment builds on those that have already been delivered. The model is iterative in nature and
focuses on the delivery of an operational product with each increment. Early increments are
stripped down versions of the final product, but they do provide capability that serves the user and
also provide a platform for evaluation by the user.

answer.explanation: Waterfall should be used only when requirements are well understood and unlikely to change radically. Rapid requirement change violates this selection condition.

choices.explanation: Available expertise is not the documented contraindication. See PDF p. 20.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Unambiguous stable requirements support, rather than undermine, the model. See PDF p. 20.

evidence.quote: Classical waterfall separates planned phases with reviewed deliverables. It fits well-understood, stable requirements and familiar technology; late feedback makes changes costly. It does not make change physically impossible: real projects revisit work under control, and modified waterfall explicitly includes feedback. Rigidity offers milestone visibility but can freeze incorrect assumptions.

options.text: Separate people can work on each sub-divided part

options.label: B
options.text: Opportunities arise for making the component reusable

options.label: C
options.text: Each individual component is smaller, and therefore easier to understand
