answer.text: Replacing or changing a component is difficult because it affects other parts extremely
answer.explanation: Subsystems can be assigned to separate teams, reused and changed with reduced impact when coupled loosely. D contradicts the change-isolation goal of good modularization.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Independent teams can realize different manageable subsystems. See PDF p. 118, 116, 32, 120.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Reusable self-contained modules are an explicit OO benefit. See PDF p. 118, 116, 32, 120.

choices.label: C

choices.label: D

evidence.quote: Logical cohesion groups similar-category operations, often selected by a flag; temporal cohesion groups operations done at the same time; functional cohesion focuses on one task. Splitting an unrelated three-purpose component improves modularity. If behavior is preserved, the restructuring is refactoring; the words are not mutually exclusive answers. Smaller modules can aid understanding, independent work, reuse and maintenance, but too many interfaces also create complexity.

module_refs.title: Software Engineering module
module_refs.quote:
6.1.1. Subsystems and classes
In order to reduce the complexity of the application domain, we identified smaller parts called
classes and organized them into packages. Similarly, to reduce the complexity of the solution
domain, we decompose a system into simpler parts, called subsystems, which are made of a
number of solution domain classes. In the case of complex subsystems, we recursively apply this
principle and decompose a subsystem into simpler subsystems (see Figure 6.2).

module_refs.title: Software Engineering module
module_refs.quote:
A class in an object-oriented system carefully delineates between its interfaces the routines and
attributes within a class are held together tightly. In a properly designed system, the classes will
be grouped into subsystems but remain independent; therefore, changing one class has no impact
on other classes, and so, the impact is minimized. However, the object-oriented approach is not a
panacea; nothing is magical here that will promote perfect design or perfect code.
Promotion of reusability
Objects are reusable because they are modeled directly out of a real-world problem domain. Each
object stands by itself or within a small circle of peers (other objects). Within this framework, the
class does not concern itself with the rest of the system or how it is going to be used within a
particular system.

module_refs.title: Software Engineering module
module_refs.quote:
6.1.3. Coupling and coherence
Coupling is the strength of dependencies between two subsystems. If two subsystems are loosely
coupled, they are relatively independent, and thus, modifications to one of the subsystems will
have little impact on the other. If two subsystems are strongly coupled, modifications to one
subsystem is likely to have impact on the other. A desirable property of a subsystem decomposition
is that subsystems are as loosely coupled as possible. This minimizes the impact that errors or
future changes have on the correct operation of the system.

questions.stem: For this project, planned testing effort in hours is setup + (cases × hours per case). The estimates (setup,cases,hours/case) are Unit=(4,80,0.1), Acceptance=(3,10,1), System=(6,20,0.5), Integration=(4,20,0.5). Which level has the greatest planned effort?
questions.hint: Use the effort formula given in the question separately for every level, then compare all computed totals.
sources: Computer Science Exit Exam practice collection · Question 13

answer.explanation: The estimates give unit effort 4+80×0.1=12 hours, acceptance 3+10×1=13, system 6+20×0.5=16, and integration 4+20×0.5=14. System testing therefore has the greatest planned effort for this project. The note does not make any test level universally longest; the explicit workload and setup assumptions are what justify this particular ranking.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Unit totals twelve hours, below the maximum.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Acceptance totals thirteen hours, below the maximum.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: System totals sixteen hours, the largest estimate.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Integration totals fourteen hours, below system testing.

evidence.quote: Unit testing isolates a function, class or small component, often replacing dependencies with stubs/mocks; a driver invokes the unit and a stub substitutes a called dependency. Integration testing exercises interfaces and interactions among combined parts. System testing checks the complete integrated system against functional and nonfunctional requirements in a representative environment.
None of these levels is universally the longest.
Planning is continuous: identify scope/deliverables, decompose work, estimate effort/duration/cost, assign resources, sequence dependencies and revise as evidence changes.

module_refs.title: Software Engineering module
module_refs.quote:
Unit testing focuses on the building blocks of the software system, that is, objects and subsystems.
There are three motivations behind focusing on components. First, unit testing reduces the
complexity of the overall test activities, allowing us to focus on smaller units of the system.
Second, unit testing makes it easier to pinpoint and correct faults, given that few components are
involved in the test. Third, unit testing allows parallelism in the testing activities; that is, each
component can be tested independently of one another.

questions.stem: A filled composition diamond is at Car’s end of its Engine association. In this model Engine remains owned for its entire lifetime and cannot be detached or transferred. What does this imply?

options.label: B
options.text: Engine can exist independently of the Car

options.label: C
options.text: Engine is part of Car and cannot exist independently under the stated lifetime policy.

questions.hint: Match the information to be represented with each model’s purpose. Read relationship direction, boundary and ownership conditions before classifying it.

answer.text: Engine is part of Car and cannot exist independently under the stated lifetime policy.
answer.explanation: Composition makes Engine a strongly owned part of Car, with the filled diamond beside the whole. Parts still owned are destroyed when their composite is destroyed. Since this model does not permit Engine to detach or transfer, it cannot continue an independent lifetime without Car. Temporary use would be a dependency, and inheritance would be shown by a hollow triangle.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Temporary use is a dependency rather than composition.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: The no-detachment policy excludes an independent Engine lifetime.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Engine is Car’s owned part and cannot outlive it under this policy.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Inheritance uses a hollow triangle.

evidence.quote: Composition uses a filled diamond at the whole end and strong ownership: a part is in at most one composite at a time, and parts still owned are destroyed with that composite. Parts may be detached/transferred under a defined model. Thus “cannot ever exist independently” is an oversimplification. For Car composing Engine, the diamond belongs beside Car; saying it points to Engine is imprecise. The Car–Engine example describes composition.

options.text: model is simple and easy to understand and use

Not suitable for projects where requirements are at a moderate to high risk of

answer.text: Poor suitability when requirements have substantial change risk.
answer.explanation: SE03 says waterfall fits stable understood requirements and familiar technology. Late feedback can make changes costly, so moderate-to-high requirement-change risk is a direct disadvantage. Simplicity and milestone visibility are advantages. Sequential phase organization characterizes the classical model; it can contribute to rigidity, but C explicitly identifies the adverse scenario asked for.

choices.explanation: Manageable milestones can be an advantage of planned rigidity, despite its trade-offs.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Likely requirement changes make late feedback and rigid commitments costly.

It does not make change physically impossible: real projects revisit work under control, and modified waterfall explicitly includes feedback. questions.stem: For a search service whose functions and database technology are already specified, which requirement adds a quantitative service-speed target?

options.label: A
options.text: The system allow user to generate PDF report.

options.label: B
options.text: The system respond to user’s request within 2 second under normal load

options.label: C
options.text: The system allow user to store data on relational database

options.label: D
options.text: The system allow user to submit emergency report

questions.hint: Distinguish observable services, measurable qualities and implementation constraints. Check scope, stakeholder meaning and the requested level of specificity.

answer.text: The system respond to user’s request within 2 second under normal load
answer.explanation: The two-second response obligation bounds the speed of a service under the stated load, so it is a performance requirement. Generating a PDF and submitting an emergency report describe services the system provides. The database clause describes storage behavior together with an implementation choice; it does not impose a response-time threshold. The explicit performance scope removes the broader taxonomy overlap between nonfunctional requirements and technology constraints.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Report generation specifies a service, not its response-time limit.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: A two-second response bound under normal load is a quantitative speed target.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: This specifies storage behavior and a database technology, without a timing bound.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Submitting an emergency report specifies a function rather than its speed.

evidence.quote: Nonfunctional requirements include quality attributes and constraints. Performance concerns response time, throughput and resource use; reliability concerns failure-free service; availability concerns being ready for use; usability concerns task success and ease of learning. Security concerns protection; compatibility concerns cooperating environments; portability concerns moving environments; maintainability/supportability concern change, diagnosis and evolution.

“Search responds within two seconds under 100 concurrent users” is measurable performance. “New users finish checkout within one minute without help” is usability. “Use Java” is a technology/pseudo-requirement, often separately classified as a system constraint. Dependability includes reliability, safety and robustness; portability is not its usual central category. Performance degradation at peak load primarily concerns performance, not automatically reliability.

questions.stem:
Which one of the following UML building block that defines the static part of the model 
and represents physical and conceptual elements?
questions.hint: Match the information to be represented with each model’s purpose. Read relationship direction, boundary and ownership conditions before classifying it.

answer.explanation: SE17 explicitly describes structural things as conceptual or physical structural elements. They make up the static model in contrast with behavior over time. Behavioral things cover dynamic aspects, grouping organizes elements and annotations add explanatory information rather than being the static elements themselves. Thus A directly matches both parts of the definition.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Structural things are the static conceptual or physical building blocks described.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Behavioral things concern dynamic behavior rather than the static structural elements.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Annotations add explanatory information rather than defining the static structural building blocks.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Grouping organizes model elements rather than being the stated conceptual/physical structural category.

evidence.quote: A class box lists name, attributes and operations; + public, - private, # protected and ~ package indicate visibility. A class diagram shows static types and relationships, while an object diagram shows particular instances/links. UML is maintained and standardized by OMG; it is a modeling language, not a lifecycle process. Structural things describe conceptual or physical structural elements.

In the course’s UML building-block terminology, structural things describe static conceptual or physical elements. Behavioral things describe dynamic interactions and state behavior. Grouping things organize model elements into packages. Annotational things attach explanatory remarks or constraints, usually as notes.

questions.stem: What is the difference between functional and non-functional requirements? Give an example of each.
questions.hint: Distinguish observable services, measurable qualities and implementation constraints. Check scope, stakeholder meaning and the requested level of specificity.

answer.text: Functional requirements specify observable behavior; nonfunctional requirements specify qualities or constraints. Example: generate a PDF report versus respond within two seconds under a stated load.
answer.explanation: SE09 includes required and prohibited services, so generating a PDF report is functional. SE10 specifies qualities such as performance, usability and availability; a response-time threshold under defined load is nonfunctional. Security mechanisms can implement functional behavior as well as support quality goals, so a negative or security-related statement is not automatically nonfunctional.

evidence.quote: A functional requirement states an observable service or behavior, including reactions to inputs, errors and forbidden actions. “When the sensor detects intrusion, send an alert” is functional.

“The system shall generate a PDF report” is functional. “The system shall not reveal another customer’s balance” can be a security-related functional rule. Security as a broad quality goal and the functions implementing it must be distinguished.

Nonfunctional requirements include quality attributes and constraints. Performance concerns response time, throughput and resource use; reliability concerns failure-free service; availability concerns being ready for use; usability concerns task success and ease of learning.
“Search responds within two seconds under 100 concurrent users” is measurable performance. “New users finish checkout within one minute without help” is usability.

questions.stem: Why is low coupling considered good in software design?
questions.hint: Separate responsibilities inside a component from dependencies across boundaries. Evaluate the stated structure, change and reuse goals without assuming guaranteed benefits.

answer.text: Low coupling limits dependencies, so changes remain local and modules are easier to understand, replace, test and maintain.
answer.explanation: SE22 measures coupling through dependencies between modules and recommends low coupling with high cohesion. Shared mutable data and knowledge of another module’s representation increase the chance that one change affects others. Stable interfaces and information hiding constrain that impact. More interfaces can add complexity, so minimizing harmful dependencies matters more than simply maximizing the number of modules.

evidence.quote: Cohesion measures how well elements inside a module serve a related purpose; coupling measures dependency between modules. Seek high cohesion and low coupling. Shared mutable data and knowledge of another module’s internal representation increase coupling. Information hiding exposes stable operations while concealing changeable decisions.

questions.stem: What is the difference between Waterfall and Agile methodologies?
questions.hint: Identify whether the scenario prioritizes delivery, learning, adaptation or risk reduction. Several processes can share individual practices, so compare their defining emphasis.

answer.text: Waterfall uses planned, reviewed stages and suits stable requirements; Agile emphasizes collaboration, working results, feedback and adaptation.
answer.explanation: SE03 describes planned phases with costly late feedback, useful for stable requirements and familiar technology. SE05 values customer participation and adaptation with useful working increments. Agile still plans and documents; waterfall can revisit work under control. The practical difference is feedback and commitment organization, not a claim that one process forbids change or the other forbids documentation.

evidence.quote: Classical waterfall separates planned phases with reviewed deliverables. It fits well-understood, stable requirements and familiar technology; late feedback makes changes costly. It does not make change physically impossible: real projects revisit work under control, and modified waterfall explicitly includes feedback. Rigidity offers milestone visibility but can freeze incorrect assumptions.

Agile favors people collaborating, useful working results, customer participation and adaptation over rigid adherence to procedures, exhaustive documents, contracts or fixed plans. The latter still have value. Agile does not mean no planning or no documentation. A user story states a small user need and value, supported by acceptance criteria; an epic groups broader work.

questions.stem: What is the difference between <<include>> and <<extend>> in use case diagrams?
questions.hint: Match the information to be represented with each model’s purpose. Read relationship direction, boundary and ownership conditions before classifying it.

answer.text: Include factors required reused behavior, with base→included; extend adds conditional behavior, with extension→base.
answer.explanation: SE16 uses include for reused required behavior incorporated when the inclusion point is reached. Extend adds behavior at extension points under a condition, and the base remains meaningful independently. The dashed arrows have different directions: including use case toward included, and extending use case toward base. Neither relation should be confused with actor association or specialization generalization.

evidence.quote: Include factors required reused behavior: Submit Order includes Validate Order, with the dashed arrow from the including/base use case to the included one. Extend adds conditional behavior at extension points: Apply Discount extends Checkout, with the arrow from the extension to the base. The base is meaningful independently. For an extension, draw the arrow from the extending use case to the base use case.

Generalization relates a specialized actor/use case to a more general one, with a hollow triangle toward the general element. An abstract use case specifies behavior for specialization and is not directly instantiated as a complete use case. It is not defined merely by reuse or lack of a direct actor line. Included behavior is incorporated where the inclusion is reached; do not infer every conditional branch in the base always executes.

questions.stem: Why is maintenance often the most expensive phase of the SDLC?
questions.hint: Classify the motive for the change before its implementation: repair, environment, useful capability or reduced future risk.

answer.text: Maintenance can dominate cost because it lasts years and repeatedly requires legacy understanding, changes, regression testing and release work.
answer.explanation: SE40 says maintenance often spans years and includes understanding existing code plus regression effort. Work is not limited to bug fixes: environments, useful capabilities and future risks also change. Repeated impact analysis, implementation and testing accumulate across the operational lifetime, so maintenance may dominate lifecycle cost. This is a common outcome, not a guarantee for every project.

evidence.quote: Corrective maintenance fixes faults; adaptive maintenance responds to environment changes; perfective maintenance improves useful capability/performance; preventive maintenance reduces future risk, such as restructuring fragile code. Motive determines category; refactoring can support preventive or perfective work. Maintenance often lasts years and includes understanding legacy code and regression effort, so it may dominate lifecycle cost.

A typical evolution sequence is change request→impact analysis→release planning→implementation/testing→release. Among a list lacking the request step, impact analysis may be the earliest listed technical activity. Major restructuring is reengineering; if the architecture itself changes, architectural transformation is the more specific description. Markets, technology, stakeholders and funding can all change scope or priorities.

questions.stem: Which software development approach emphasizes breaking systems into functions or procedures that manipulate isolated data?
questions.hint: Identify whether the scenario prioritizes delivery, learning, adaptation or risk reduction. Several processes can share individual practices, so compare their defining emphasis.

answer.explanation: SE01 contrasts procedural decomposition organized around functions with object-oriented decomposition organized around objects combining state and behavior. B is the available traditional/procedural label for functions operating on data. Agile and iterative describe lifecycle organization rather than this decomposition paradigm, and either can be used with procedural or object-oriented programming.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Object orientation combines state and behavior in objects rather than organizing primarily around separate procedures.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Traditional/procedural decomposition organizes functions and procedures acting on data.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Agile concerns process adaptation rather than requiring function-based decomposition.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Iteration describes revisiting development work and does not determine procedural versus object decomposition.

evidence.quote: Procedural decomposition organizes functions; object oriented decomposition organizes objects with state and behavior. Either can use iterative or sequential development. OOP does not automatically shorten every project. Reuse, encapsulation and consistent models can reduce duplication and ease change; poor object design can still be complex. Functional programming emphasizes function evaluation and controlled side effects; event-driven programs react to events.

questions.stem: In the Object-Oriented Approach, which property allows classes to be used in different parts of the system or other projects without rewriting them?
questions.hint: Separate responsibilities inside a component from dependencies across boundaries. Evaluate the stated structure, change and reuse goals without assuming guaranteed benefits.

answer.explanation: The stem explicitly asks about using existing classes elsewhere without rewriting them, which is reuse. SE01 lists reuse alongside encapsulation and consistent models as ways to reduce duplication and ease change. Encapsulation and abstraction can make reuse safer, while polymorphism supports compatible varying implementations, but those are enabling concepts rather than the name of the capability described.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Encapsulation hides implementation and can enable reuse, but it is not the capability's name.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Polymorphism supports differing implementations through compatible interfaces rather than directly naming reuse.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Reusability means using suitable existing classes or components in other contexts without rewriting them.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Abstraction exposes relevant contracts and can assist reuse, but the requested property is reusability.

evidence.quote: Encapsulation groups state with operations and hides representation behind an interface. Polymorphism permits different object types to respond differently through a common operation or interface. Abstraction exposes the relevant contract while omitting unnecessary detail. Reusability means using suitable existing classes or components in new contexts rather than writing them again. These ideas support each other but name different properties.

questions.stem: Which of the four fundamental software process activities involves making updates to meet changing customer needs after deployment?
questions.hint: Classify the motive for the change before its implementation: repair, environment, useful capability or reduced future risk.

answer.explanation: SE40 describes maintenance and evolution through change requests, impact analysis, planning, implementation/testing and release. Updating a deployed product to meet changing customer needs belongs to evolution among the four broad process activities. Specification, implementation and validation still occur within that work, but D names the lifecycle-wide change activity asked for rather than one constituent task.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Specification captures needs but does not name the overall postdeployment change activity.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Design/implementation is part of making a change rather than the broad evolution activity.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Validation checks the changed product against needs rather than naming ongoing adaptation itself.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Evolution updates existing software as stakeholder needs and operating conditions change.

evidence.quote: Corrective maintenance fixes faults; adaptive maintenance responds to environment changes; perfective maintenance improves useful capability/performance; preventive maintenance reduces future risk, such as restructuring fragile code. Motive determines category; refactoring can support preventive or perfective work. Maintenance often lasts years and includes understanding legacy code and regression effort, so it may dominate lifecycle cost.
A typical evolution sequence is change request→impact analysis→release planning→implementation/testing→release.

questions.stem: A software process that plans all activities in advance and measures progress against that plan is classified as:
questions.hint: Identify whether the scenario prioritizes delivery, learning, adaptation or risk reduction. Several processes can share individual practices, so compare their defining emphasis.

answer.explanation: The stem defines up-front planning and measurement against that plan. B names the plan-driven organization, illustrated by SE03’s planned phases and reviewed deliverables. Incremental delivery and evolution describe how results grow or change and can coexist with planning. Agile also plans, but it emphasizes adaptation rather than defining all activity commitments in advance as stated here.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Agile uses planning but adapts content as feedback arrives rather than defining this fixed up-front emphasis.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Plan-driven explicitly organizes activities and progress measurement around an advance plan.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Incremental describes staged capability delivery and does not alone specify up-front planning commitments.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Evolutionary describes progressive change rather than necessarily advance planning of all activities.

evidence.quote: In a plan-driven process, activities are planned in advance and progress is assessed against that plan. Agile planning is incremental and adapts to changing needs. This distinction concerns planning strategy; a process can combine advance planning with staged deliveries and feedback.

questions.stem: In requirement elicitation, the document created to describe what the system should do — agreed upon by clients and developers — is called:
questions.hint: Distinguish observable services, measurable qualities and implementation constraints. Check scope, stakeholder meaning and the requested level of specificity.

answer.explanation: SE08 states that the Software Requirements Specification organizes agreed requirements. That is the artifact describing what the system should do for client/developer agreement. Analysis models support technical discussion, a use-case diagram captures only selected goals/relationships and a design document describes solution decisions. None replaces the overall agreed requirements specification.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Analysis models formalize selected aspects for discussion rather than replacing the full agreed requirements document.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: A use-case diagram shows goals and roles but not the complete requirements specification.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: The requirements specification organizes the agreed services and constraints the system must satisfy.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: A design document describes how the solution is organized rather than the complete statement of required behavior.

evidence.quote: Business requirements explain why the project exists and its goals. User requirements describe stakeholder needs at a useful high level; system requirements specify detailed services and constraints. The Software Requirements Specification (SRS) organizes the agreed requirements. A natural-language specification communicates with clients while analysis models formalize it for technical discussion; real specifications can also contain diagrams.

questions.stem: What is the key distinction between a Requirements Specification and an Analysis Model?

options.label: A
options.text: The specification uses diagrams; the model uses natural language

options.label: B
options.text: The specification uses natural language; the model uses symbols and diagrams

options.label: C
options.text: Both use the same representation but serve different purposes

options.label: D
options.text: The analysis model is only for developers; specification is for testing

questions.hint: Distinguish observable services, measurable qualities and implementation constraints. Check scope, stakeholder meaning and the requested level of specificity.

answer.text: In the taught convention, natural-language client specification versus symbolic/diagrammatic analysis models.
answer.explanation: SE08 explicitly describes natural-language specification for clients and analysis models that formalize it for technical discussion. B matches that teaching convention. This is not a universal ban on diagrams in an SRS: the note immediately allows them in real specifications. The other choices reverse the convention or impose unsupported exclusive audiences and purposes.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: It reverses the natural-language specification versus formalized-model convention taught in the note.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: This matches the taught convention, while real requirements specifications can also include diagrams.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: The taught distinction does use different representation emphases rather than identical forms.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Neither artifact has the exclusive audience or testing-only purpose asserted here.

evidence.quote: Business requirements explain why the project exists and its goals. User requirements describe stakeholder needs at a useful high level; system requirements specify detailed services and constraints. The Software Requirements Specification (SRS) organizes the agreed requirements. A natural-language specification communicates with clients while analysis models formalize it for technical discussion; real specifications can also contain diagrams.

questions.stem: In use case modeling, actors can be defined as:

options.label: A
options.text: Only human users who interact with the system

options.label: B
options.text: People, machines, or external systems that interact with the system

options.label: C
options.text: Only primary users who need system assistance

options.label: D
options.text: Software components within the system boundary

questions.hint: Match the information to be represented with each model’s purpose. Read relationship direction, boundary and ownership conditions before classifying it.

answer.text: External interacting roles played by people, devices or other systems.
answer.explanation: SE14 explicitly permits a person, device or other system to play an external actor role. B is the only option including those categories. Actors are not restricted to primary users or humans, and internal components are inside the chosen system boundary rather than external roles. One person may play several actors, so actor instances should not be confused with individual people.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Actors can be devices or external systems as well as human users.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: People, devices and external systems can play roles interacting across the system boundary.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Supporting and administrative external roles can be actors, not only primary goal-seeking users.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Internal components are not external actor roles under the chosen system boundary.

evidence.quote: Draw actors outside the system boundary rectangle and use-case ovals inside. Name a goal with a verb and noun. The diagram shows roles, goals and relationships, not the full detailed algorithm or UI layout. Being an internal component is different from being an external actor; the chosen boundary determines which role applies.
An actor is an external role interacting with the system; it can be a person, device or another system.

questions.stem: Which type of requirement specifies that 'the system must respond within 1 second'?
questions.hint: Distinguish observable services, measurable qualities and implementation constraints. Check scope, stakeholder meaning and the requested level of specificity.

answer.explanation: SE10 identifies response time as a performance quality. A one-second threshold constrains how well a service responds rather than naming the service itself, so C is the appropriate category. A complete measurable requirement should also define the operation, load and timing conditions. Those omissions affect test precision, not the underlying classification of the stated response-time target.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: The statement constrains response speed rather than specifying which service is performed.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: The specific quality is performance; this is not primarily a technology or implementation constraint.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: The one-second limit is a nonfunctional response-time/performance target.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: No domain-specific business rule is stated; the obligation concerns a general performance quality.

evidence.quote: Nonfunctional requirements include quality attributes and constraints. Performance concerns response time, throughput and resource use; reliability concerns failure-free service; availability concerns being ready for use; usability concerns task success and ease of learning. Security concerns protection; compatibility concerns cooperating environments; portability concerns moving environments; maintainability/supportability concern change, diagnosis and evolution.

questions.stem: When technology constraints are separated from quality attributes, what is the most specific category for “the system must be built using Java”?
questions.hint: Distinguish observable services, measurable qualities and implementation constraints. Check scope, stakeholder meaning and the requested level of specificity.

answer.explanation: The statement prescribes an implementation technology rather than an externally observable service or a measurable product quality. In the course’s explicit separation of quality attributes from technology constraints, the specific category is a system or constraint requirement. A broad requirements taxonomy can place constraints under nonfunctional requirements, but the question asks for the more specific category. No performance, reliability or usability threshold is supplied by merely naming Java.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: The statement prescribes technology rather than an observable service.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: This is a broader umbrella in some taxonomies; it is incomplete when the specific constraint category is offered.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: A required implementation language is a technology or system constraint.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: No measurable quality attribute is specified merely by requiring Java.

evidence.quote: “Search responds within two seconds under 100 concurrent users” is measurable performance. “New users finish checkout within one minute without help” is usability. “Use Java” is a technology/pseudo-requirement, often separately classified as a system constraint. Dependability includes reliability, safety and robustness; portability is not its usual central category. Performance degradation at peak load primarily concerns performance, not automatically reliability.

questions.stem: Which nonfunctional requirement category addresses the ability of the system to work across different web browsers and devices?
questions.hint: Distinguish observable services, measurable qualities and implementation constraints. Check scope, stakeholder meaning and the requested level of specificity.

answer.explanation: SE10 distinguishes compatibility, which concerns cooperating environments, from portability, which concerns moving environments. Supporting different browsers and devices in the question is the offered compatibility category. Reliability concerns failure-free service, scalability concerns growth and usability concerns task success/ease of learning. None of those names the stated cross-environment cooperation requirement as directly.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Reliability concerns failure-free service rather than which browsers and devices can cooperate with the system.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Scalability concerns handling increased workload rather than cross-browser/device compatibility.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Usability concerns ease of learning and successful tasks, not the supported environment set itself.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Compatibility addresses operating/cooperating across the specified browsers and device environments.

evidence.quote: Nonfunctional requirements include quality attributes and constraints. Performance concerns response time, throughput and resource use; reliability concerns failure-free service; availability concerns being ready for use; usability concerns task success and ease of learning. Security concerns protection; compatibility concerns cooperating environments; portability concerns moving environments; maintainability/supportability concern change, diagnosis and evolution.

Scalability is the ability to accommodate additional workload while maintaining the required service, often by increasing available resources. It concerns growth in demand. Compatibility concerns supported cooperating environments, such as browsers and devices; usability concerns successful and learnable user tasks.

questions.stem: Dependability in software engineering is a broader concept that includes all of the following EXCEPT:
questions.hint: Distinguish observable services, measurable qualities and implementation constraints. Check scope, stakeholder meaning and the requested level of specificity.

answer.text: Portability is the exception to the usual central dependability categories.
answer.explanation: SE10 explicitly includes reliability, safety and robustness in dependability and says portability is not its usual central category. Portability instead concerns moving environments. Thus D is the listed exception. The distinction does not imply portability never affects practical service outcomes, only that it is a different quality category from the taught dependability grouping.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Reliability is explicitly included in the taught dependability grouping.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Robustness is explicitly included in the broader dependability concept.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Safety is explicitly included among dependability concerns.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Portability concerns moving environments rather than the usual central dependability categories.

evidence.quote: Dependability includes reliability, safety and robustness; portability is not its usual central category.
Security concerns protection; compatibility concerns cooperating environments; portability concerns moving environments; maintainability/supportability concern change, diagnosis and evolution.
Robustness concerns reliable operation across varied or difficult operating conditions and controlled failure outside the supported range.

questions.stem: In requirements elicitation activities, which step involves formalizing scenarios into structured descriptions of system interactions?
questions.hint: Distinguish observable services, measurable qualities and implementation constraints. Check scope, stakeholder meaning and the requested level of specificity.

answer.text: Identifying use cases by abstracting concrete scenarios.
answer.explanation: SE13 calls a scenario one concrete execution and a use case an abstraction of related success and alternative scenarios. Formalizing those interactions into the more general use-case description therefore identifies use cases. Identifying actors establishes external roles, identifying scenarios captures individual executions and later refinement adds detail to an already identified use case.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Actor identification establishes external roles rather than generalizing scenario executions into interaction descriptions.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Use cases abstract related concrete scenarios into structured goal-oriented interaction descriptions.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Scenario identification captures concrete executions rather than their use-case abstraction.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Refinement elaborates an existing use case; the scenario-to-use-case abstraction is the identification step asked here.

evidence.quote: A scenario is one concrete execution; a use case abstracts the related successful and alternative scenarios. Analysis integrates functional (use cases/scenarios), structural/object (classes) and dynamic (states/interactions) models. Entity objects represent domain information such as Incident; boundary objects mediate interaction, such as ReportForm; control objects coordinate a use case. A UI form is normally boundary, not entity.

questions.stem: According to the Simple Use Case Writing Guide, which of the following is CORRECT practice?

options.label: A
options.text: Use passive voice so responsibility is unclear

options.label: B
options.text: Describe user interface elements in detail

options.label: C
options.text: Document exceptions separately from the main flow

options.label: D
options.text: Combine multiple tasks into one use case for brevity

questions.hint: Match the information to be represented with each model’s purpose. Read relationship direction, boundary and ownership conditions before classifying it.

answer.text: Document exceptions separately from the main success flow.
answer.explanation: SE15 instructs writers to use active subject–verb steps and separate errors from normal flow. C follows that rule directly. Passive voice hides responsibility, detailed UI design distracts from goal-level behavior, and combining unrelated tasks does not produce a clear use case. The distinction concerns organizing scenarios rather than omitting exception handling.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Passive voice makes responsibility less clear, contrary to the active subject–verb guideline.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Detailed UI elements are not the goal-level behavior and flow structure emphasized by the guide.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Separating exception behavior keeps the main success flow clear while still documenting failures.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Combining multiple unrelated tasks sacrifices a coherent goal and consistent abstraction level.

evidence.quote: Example: Submit Incident. Precondition: officer authenticated. 1 Officer supplies location and description. 2 System validates details. 3 System records the incident. 4 System returns its ID. Alternative 2a: location missing → report the problem and request correction; save nothing. Success postcondition: incident and ID persist; failure guarantee: no partial record. An alternate flow is a conditional variation; an exception flow handles a failure. Preconditions hold before entry, while a trigger starts the use case.
Use active subject–verb steps at one abstraction level; separate errors from the normal flow.

questions.stem: In the FAST (Facilitated Application Specification Technique), participants are initially asked to individually create lists of three item categories. Which is NOT one of them?

options.label: A
options.text: Things that are part of the environment surrounding the system

options.label: B
options.text: Things the system produces or outputs

options.label: D
options.text: Things the system uses or takes as inputs

questions.hint: Distinguish observable services, measurable qualities and implementation constraints. Check scope, stakeholder meaning and the requested level of specificity.

answer.text: Technical risks and constraints are not one of the three initial FAST lists.
answer.explanation: SE12 explicitly lists environment elements, outputs and inputs as the initial participant categories. A, B and D match them. Technical risks and constraints can matter elsewhere in engineering, but they are not one of those three named initial FAST lists. The negative question asks about that procedure, not whether risk information is ever useful.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Environment elements are explicitly one of the initial FAST categories.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: System outputs are explicitly included in the three initial lists.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Risks and constraints are not one of the specified environment/output/input categories.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Inputs and things the system uses are part of the stated initial categories.

evidence.quote: In the taught FAST technique, participants list environment elements, outputs and inputs, consolidate lists and develop smaller specifications. QFD prioritizes customer value: normal needs are explicitly stated, expected needs are assumed, and exciting needs provide unanticipated benefit. Brainstorm first to generate ideas, then evaluate and prioritize; do not confuse that with letting every idea become a committed requirement.

questions.stem: In Quality Function Deployment (QFD), which category of requirements represents features that go beyond customer expectations and provide great satisfaction?
questions.hint: Distinguish observable services, measurable qualities and implementation constraints. Check scope, stakeholder meaning and the requested level of specificity.

answer.explanation: SE12 distinguishes explicitly stated normal needs, assumed expected needs and exciting needs that bring unanticipated benefit. Features exceeding expectations and producing additional satisfaction match the exciting category. Calling them merely implicit would confuse customer assumptions with unexpected added value rather than identify the QFD term.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Normal requirements are explicitly stated needs rather than unexpected extra benefits.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Expected requirements are assumed by customers and do not denote surprising added satisfaction.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Exciting requirements deliver unanticipated benefit beyond the customer’s expectations.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Implicit describes assumed needs more generally, not the QFD category for unanticipated benefits.

evidence.quote: In the taught FAST technique, participants list environment elements, outputs and inputs, consolidate lists and develop smaller specifications. QFD prioritizes customer value: normal needs are explicitly stated, expected needs are assumed, and exciting needs provide unanticipated benefit. Brainstorm first to generate ideas, then evaluate and prioritize; do not confuse that with letting every idea become a committed requirement.

questions.stem: Which validation property ensures that the requirements specification does not contain contradictory statements?
questions.hint: Distinguish observable services, measurable qualities and implementation constraints. Check scope, stakeholder meaning and the requested level of specificity.

answer.explanation: SE11 directly defines consistency as excluding contradictions. Completeness covers agreed scope, clarity gives one intended interpretation, and correctness reflects stakeholder needs. A specification can be complete yet inconsistent, or clear yet wrong, so these properties cannot substitute for the precise no-contradictions condition.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Completeness concerns covering scope and behavior, not whether requirements contradict each other.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Consistency requires the specification’s statements to coexist without contradiction.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Clarity addresses interpretive ambiguity rather than logical compatibility between requirements.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Correctness concerns actual stakeholder needs, a different validation property.

evidence.quote: Correct requirements reflect actual stakeholder needs. Complete requirements address the agreed scope, normal and exceptional behavior. Consistency excludes contradictions. questions.stem: The Waterfall model is MOST appropriate when:

options.label: A
options.text: Requirements are expected to change frequently during development

options.label: B
options.text: The project is large and complex with evolving needs

options.label: C
options.text: Requirements are constant, the project is short, and technology is stable

options.label: D
options.text: The team needs to deliver working software in small increments

questions.hint: Identify whether the scenario prioritizes delivery, learning, adaptation or risk reduction. Several processes can share individual practices, so compare their defining emphasis.

answer.text: Stable requirements and familiar, stable technology.
answer.explanation: SE03 says classical waterfall fits well-understood stable requirements and familiar technology, directly supporting C among these alternatives. Frequent change, evolving needs and early small deliveries call for feedback or incremental capability rather than waterfall’s late feedback. Short duration alone is not a proof, but C also supplies the decisive stability conditions stated in the note.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Frequent requirement changes make late-feedback sequential planning a poor fit.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Large evolving needs do not establish the stable requirements that favor classical waterfall.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Constant requirements and stable technology match the note’s stated waterfall selection conditions.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Prioritized usable small deliveries are the rationale for incremental delivery rather than a single sequential release.

evidence.quote: Classical waterfall separates planned phases with reviewed deliverables. It fits well-understood, stable requirements and familiar technology; late feedback makes changes costly. It does not make change physically impossible: real projects revisit work under control, and modified waterfall explicitly includes feedback. Rigidity offers milestone visibility but can freeze incorrect assumptions.

answer.explanation: Classical waterfall separates planned phases and may receive important feedback late. Correcting earlier assumptions can then require costly rework across completed deliverables, which is its characteristic drawback here. Changes are still possible under control. Skilled developers are needed across approaches, and waterfall provides milestone visibility and documentation, so the other alternatives do not identify the stated comparative disadvantage.

choices.label: C

choices.label: D

questions.stem: What is the key conceptual distinction between iteration and incremental delivery, even when a process combines both?

options.label: D

questions.hint: Identify whether the scenario prioritizes delivery, learning, adaptation or risk reduction. Several processes can share individual practices, so compare their defining emphasis.

answer.text: Iteration revisits and improves a solution; an increment adds usable functionality.
answer.explanation: Iteration revisits and improves a solution, while an increment adds usable functionality. A process can refine existing capability and add new capability in the same cycle, so the concepts are compatible but not identical. Neither requires rebuilding the entire system or making every increment completely independent. Risk analysis is a separate concern rather than the structural distinction defining these two terms.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: This reverses refinement and added functionality.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Iteration refines; increments add usable capability.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: The terms differ even when combined in one process.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Risk analysis does not define their distinction.

evidence.quote: Choose incremental delivery when prioritized partial capability must reach users early. Smaller changes can be easier to debug and permit feedback, though architecture and integration still require planning. Iteration need not rebuild the whole system every time, and increments need not be perfectly independent modules. Broad descriptions of early working software can fit prototypes, iterative or Agile processes; identify the purpose of that early version.
Iteration revisits and improves a solution; an increment adds usable functionality. A process may do both.

questions.stem: A large application already has its core capabilities. The main development goal is to revisit and improve that existing solution repeatedly as feedback and future changes arrive, rather than primarily add new capability in each delivery. Which concept most directly names that emphasis?
questions.hint: Identify whether the scenario prioritizes delivery, learning, adaptation or risk reduction. Several processes can share individual practices, so compare their defining emphasis.

answer.explanation: The stated emphasis is iterative: revisiting and improving an existing solution in response to feedback. Incremental development names the addition of usable functionality, which is not the primary goal specified, although both can coexist. Classical waterfall’s stable staged planning and the V-model’s paired assurance structure do not directly name this refinement emphasis. Large size and anticipated change alone would not have selected a unique model.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Classical waterfall does not directly name repeated refinement as the organizing emphasis.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: The V-model emphasizes paired development and tests.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Iteration directly names revisiting and improving the existing solution.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Incremental describes added functionality rather than the specified primary emphasis.

evidence.quote: Choose incremental delivery when prioritized partial capability must reach users early. questions.stem: In the Agile SDLC, small units of functionality that the software needs to deliver are called:

answer.explanation: SE05 defines a user story as a small user need and value supported by acceptance criteria. Sprints and iterations name cycles or timeboxes, not the need itself. An epic groups broader work. C therefore names the small functional work unit intended here, without claiming that Agile requirements consist only of story text.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: A Sprint is a timeboxed development interval rather than the individual user need.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: An iteration is a cycle of work or refinement, not a small functional requirement.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: A user story states a small user need and its value with acceptance criteria.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: An epic groups broader work rather than naming the smaller story-sized need.

evidence.quote: Scrum uses timeboxed Sprints of at most one month, with a Sprint Goal, selected work and a usable Increment meeting a Definition of Done. Scope is discussed before and during planning; it is not forbidden to agree scope. Timeboxes tend to stay fixed while content is adapted without endangering the goal. Agile can be combined with required assurance/documentation; safety-critical context alone cannot prove it is unsuitable.
A user story states a small user need and value, supported by acceptance criteria; an epic groups broader work.

questions.stem: The Spiral Model distinguishes itself from other models primarily through its emphasis on:

options.label: C
options.text: Customer delivery at the end of the project

questions.hint: Identify whether the scenario prioritizes delivery, learning, adaptation or risk reduction. Several processes can share individual practices, so compare their defining emphasis.

answer.text: Risk analysis and reduction in every spiral cycle.
answer.explanation: SE06 defines spiral development as risk driven, with each cycle identifying objectives and alternatives, assessing and reducing risks, producing a result and planning commitment. That emphasis distinguishes it from merely repeating phases or delivering only at the end. It can adapt requirements and combine other activities rather than enforcing an unchangeable initial specification.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: A spiral can contain staged work, but sequential completion is not its defining driver.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Risk assessment and reduction guide each cycle’s work and further commitment.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Only delivering at the end is not the distinguishing spiral principle.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: A risk-driven cycle can revise plans and requirements rather than rigidly freeze them.

evidence.quote: Spiral development is risk driven. Each cycle identifies objectives and alternatives, assesses and reduces important risks, develops/verifies an appropriate next result, and plans further commitment. A prototype may test a risky technology before a large investment. The amount and type of work depend on the risks.

questions.stem: The V-Model derives its name from its shape. What does the BOTTOM of the 'V' represent?
questions.hint: Identify whether the scenario prioritizes delivery, learning, adaptation or risk reduction. Several processes can share individual practices, so compare their defining emphasis.

answer.explanation: SE03 explicitly places coding at the bottom of the V while specification and design stages correspond to later testing levels. Requirements therefore begin the development side rather than occupy the bottom; deployment and maintenance are not that connecting implementation activity. This is a model-diagram convention, not a claim that all real work follows a perfect geometric sequence.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Requirements occur on the specification side, not at the coding bottom of the V.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Deployment is not the implementation activity joining the V-model’s sides.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: The note explicitly identifies coding as the bottom of the V.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Maintenance occurs in lifecycle evolution rather than at this implementation point.

evidence.quote: The V-model pairs specification/design stages with later test levels. Requirements inform acceptance tests; system design informs system tests; component/detail design informs integration/unit tests. Coding lies at the bottom. Test planning starts early. Stable requirements and strong assurance may favor this organization, but neither a V shape nor waterfall guarantees safety or correctness.

questions.stem: Which organization standardizes and maintains UML as a modeling language?
questions.hint: Match the information to be represented with each model’s purpose. Read relationship direction, boundary and ownership conditions before classifying it.

questions.stem: In a UML Use Case Diagram, the rectangle enclosing all use cases is called:

questions.stem: When execution reaches an include relationship’s inclusion point in a base use case, what does include require?

options.label: B

options.label: C
options.text: An inheritance relationship between two use cases

options.label: D
options.text: A timing constraint between two use cases

questions.hint: Match the information to be represented with each model’s purpose. Read relationship direction, boundary and ownership conditions before classifying it.

answer.text: The included behavior is required whenever execution reaches the inclusion point.
answer.explanation: Include factors required reused behavior into another use case. When the base reaches the inclusion point, the included behavior is incorporated and performed as specified. This does not imply that every possible conditional branch of the base reaches that point. Optional conditional additions correspond to extend, specialization to generalization, and timing constraints are separate from the inclusion relationship.

questions.stem: In system design, 'coupling' between subsystems refers to:

options.label: A
options.text: How well objects within a subsystem work toward a common goal

options.label: B
options.text: The number of operations a subsystem exposes

options.label: C
options.text: The degree of dependency between two subsystems

options.label: D
options.text: The architectural pattern chosen for the system

questions.hint: Separate responsibilities inside a component from dependencies across boundaries. Evaluate the stated structure, change and reuse goals without assuming guaranteed benefits.

answer.text: The degree of dependency between subsystems.
answer.explanation: SE22 explicitly distinguishes cohesion within a module from coupling between modules. A describes cohesion; C describes coupling. Interface operation count can affect design complexity but is not the definition of dependence, and an architectural pattern may influence coupling without being the relationship measure itself. The goal is usually low coupling with high cohesion.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Related purpose inside a subsystem defines cohesion rather than between-subsystem coupling.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Operation count alone does not measure the actual dependencies between subsystems.

choices.label: C

choices.label: D

evidence.quote: Cohesion measures how well elements inside a module serve a related purpose; coupling measures dependency between modules. Seek high cohesion and low coupling. questions.stem: In architectural design, a 'closed architecture' in a layered system means:

options.label: A
options.text: No external access to any layer is allowed

options.label: B
options.text: A layer can access any layer at deeper levels freely

options.label: C
options.text: A layer can only call the layer immediately below it

options.label: D
options.text: All layers communicate through a central repository

questions.hint: Separate responsibilities inside a component from dependencies across boundaries. Evaluate the stated structure, change and reuse goals without assuming guaranteed benefits.

answer.text: Calls are restricted to the immediately lower layer.

evidence.quote: A layer is a logical abstraction level; a tier is a deployment separation. A closed layered architecture permits calls only to the immediately lower layer; an open one permits approved skipping. For top-to-bottom A,B,C,D, A→B obeys closed layering, A→C skips, and lower-to-upper calls violate the simple dependency rule unless explicitly mediated by a defined mechanism.
